newsitem.title: USA: Republicans abandon Dole, fight for survival.
newsitem.headline: Republicans abandon Dole, fight for survival.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
With Bob Dole apparently heading for defeat in next week's presidential election, Republican congressional candidates are abandoning ship.

In recent weeks many have stressed their independence from Dole as well as unpopular House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich. Others sold themselves as a moderating force on President Bill Clinton.

Though they did not admit it, Republican Party chiefs were focusing most of their efforts and money on an all-out bid to preserve the slim majorities they won two years ago in the Senate and the House.
"What we're saying is, remember what Bill Clinton and a Democratic Congress are like. They are very, very liberal," Gingrich said in a television interview on Sunday.

The Republicans were running television advertisements in key districts across the nation urging voters not to give Clinton a "blank check" for his second term by restoring the Democrats control of Congress.

Another commercial shown in many districts began with an image of a woman looking into a crystal ball. "What would happen if the Democrats controlled Congress and the White House?" she muses. "Been there. Done that. Remember?"

The advertisement went on to remind voters that Clinton tried to pass an unpopular government health care plan in his first two years in office when he was backed by Democratic majorities in the House and Senate.
Some Republican candidates produced spots stressing their independence from their own party leadership and giving examples of issues on which they differed with Gingrich.
Others declined to show up for Dole rallies in their home districts, afraid even to be pictured on the same podium as their presidential nominee.
Dole's vice presidential running-mate Jack Kemp branded such party members as cowards and fair weather friends.
"It is disappointing ... to hear that some Republicans would run away at this moment of need for a man who's been a hero his whole career," he said last weekend.
"There are some Republicans who are summer soldiers and sunshine patriots," Kemp declared.
Such words meant little to scores of vulnerable Republican candidates across the country, facing their own tough struggles for political survival.

House Republicans held a 53-47 majority in the Senate and a 235-198 majority in the House. But many of those who swept into office as part of the 1994 Republicans surge were highly vulnerable as the tide ebbed.
Such politicians put their faith in polls that showed Republican congressional candidates running far ahead of Dole in a political climate that seemed to favour incumbents.
The big question was whether that would hold up Election Day.

"If Clinton wins the election by 12 points on November 5, you would have to have an awful lot of voters consciously splitting their tickets and voting for Republicans for Congress to neutralise that," said David Birdsell, a political scientist at Baruch University in New York City.
However he said Republicans had little to lose by running away from Dole since more voters than in the past were saying they wanted divided government to continue.
American University political historian Allan Lichtman said it made little difference whether Republicans ran with Dole or abandoned him.
"It's very difficult to run against your own presidential candidate," he said.

"If Clinton wins big, history suggests the effects of his victory will carry over to many congressional races. If Bob Dole loses big, that is bad news for Republican candidates across-the-board," he said.
